Where does Carol Stream sit in DuPage County?

Carol Stream is a village in DuPage County, Illinois, in the western Chicago suburbs. It was incorporated on January 5, 1959, and 39,854 people lived there at the 2020 census.

The village covers 9.44 square miles, of which 9.12 are land and 0.32 are water. That is a compact footprint for nearly 40,000 people. The village dates only from 1959, so the housing stock is young by Chicago-area standards.

  • County: DuPage, with deeds recorded at the DuPage County Recorder
  • Village government: a mayor and six trustees, with an appointed village administrator
  • Parks: 36 parks run by the Carol Stream Park District

How did Carol Stream get started?

Developer Jay Stream began buying unincorporated farmland outside Wheaton in 1957, after a frustrating run-in with red tape on a Naperville subdivision, and named the new community for his daughter Carol.

The first village board meeting took place on February 12, 1959. The population was 836 in the 1960 census, then climbed to 4,434 in 1970, 15,472 in 1980 and 31,716 in 1990. It peaked near 40,438 in 2000, slipped to 39,711 in 2010 and stood at 39,854 in 2020.

A former Gretna railway station was renamed Carol Stream in 1962 and now serves as a museum for the Carol Stream Historical Society. The pattern of fast growth followed by a flat decade is useful to a seller: most neighbors bought within the same few decades, so comparable sales tend to be houses of similar age.

Which employers shape the Carol Stream housing market?

Carol Stream's jobs lean toward warehousing, food production and printing rather than one anchor company. The village's 2022 annual financial report, as summarized in the encyclopedia entry for the village, lists these largest employers:

  • Hearthside Food Solutions, 650 employees
  • FIC America Corp., 494
  • Grunt Style, 400
  • FedEx, 369
  • American Litho, 350
  • Tyndale House Publishers, 260

The United States Postal Service also runs a sectional hub here for ZIP codes beginning 601 and 603. Because the employer base is spread across several industries, a layoff at one plant is unlikely to empty the neighborhood, though it can affect a seller who has to move on a short timeline.

Which school districts serve homes in Carol Stream?

Carol Stream's village limits do not match school district lines, so the district depends on the street address. Buyers ask about this early, and a seller who can answer it removes one question from the showing.

  • Most homes: Community Consolidated School District 93 for kindergarten through eighth grade, then Glenbard Township High School District 87 and Glenbard North High School
  • Northwest corner: Elgin Area School District U46, with Spring Trail Elementary in the village
  • Part of the west side: Benjamin School District 25, then Community High School District 94 and West Chicago Community High School
  • Some southern and southeastern blocks: Community Unit School District 200 in Wheaton, or Glen Ellyn School District 41 with Glenbard North for high school

District 93 runs eight schools in the village, including Jay Stream Middle School, named for the founder, and Stratford Middle School.

What roads and transit connect Carol Stream?

North Avenue runs east and west near the middle of the village and is the main corridor, with Army Trail Road and Geneva Road as the other major east-west routes. Gary Avenue runs north and south toward Bloomingdale and the Stratford Square area, and County Farm Road is a major commercial route. Schmale Road serves a small commercial pocket in the southeast, and Kuhn Road runs north and south as a lesser route.

Pace operates Route 711 between Carol Stream and Wheaton. The Great Western Trail crosses town, and the Steve Ravanesi Trail links it to Red Hawk Park, the dog park and Glenbard North High School. A house within a short walk of the trail or a park district facility has an easy item to put in a listing description.

What does Carol Stream require before a sale can close?

The village charges its own transfer tax, and the stamp has to be obtained before closing paperwork goes to the recorder. The rate printed on the Finance Department page is $3.00 for each $1,000 of the selling price or fraction thereof.

Carol Stream transfer stamp checklist, from the Village of Carol Stream Finance Department page
ItemWhat the village page says
Where stamps are issuedFinance Department at the village's main offices
FormsSigned transfer stamp declaration and the State of Illinois transfer declaration
ContractCopy of the fully executed contract showing the price
WaterFinal meter reading booked at least 2 working days before closing; final bill paid before the stamp is issued
Exempt deeds$25 administrative fee for exempt stamps

Contracts can be emailed to the Finance Department, with a 25MB file limit and no zip files. Call the Water Billing division at 630-871-6222 to set the meter reading. Most readings are taken by radio, so the village does not usually need to enter the house.

Who pays the village tax, and can it be refunded?

The seller, or grantor, normally owes the village tax. When a property passes through a sheriff's sale or a tax deed, the buyer owes it instead.

The village allows a refund only when every one of four conditions is met. The seller must have lived in the house for a year within the last three, must not have rented out any part of it, must have bought and now occupy a replacement home inside the village, and must apply within one year of paying the tax. A seller who moves out of Carol Stream will not qualify for this refund.

Do permits matter when I sell a Carol Stream house?

Yes, since an unclosed permit is a question a buyer's agent or the closing attorney may raise. Permit applications go through the Community Development Department, either online or in person, and the village notes a card fee of 2.9 percent online and 3.5 percent at the counter.

  • Inspections need about 24 hours of advance notice and are scheduled at 630-871-6230 between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m.
  • Plumbing inspections are done by a consultant on Monday, Wednesday and Friday afternoons, 1:30 to 3:30 p.m.
  • A re-inspection fee can apply if work fails or is not ready, and it must be paid before the next visit

If you remember a finished basement, deck or water heater swap from a previous owner, ask Community Development whether the permit was closed out. A cash buyer purchasing as-is absorbs that question, while a retail buyer's lender may want it settled.

What state and county steps apply to a sale here?

The state adds its own levy on title transfers under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, at half a dollar for each $500 of declared value. The declaration is filed through the state's MyDec system, and the Carol Stream stamp requires a copy of it.

Your deed is filed with the DuPage County Recorder, whose land records reach back to 1839. The recorder's office can be reached at 630-407-5400, and it also provides deed copies if you need one for a tax appeal or an exemption.

How do listing, selling yourself and a cash offer compare in Carol Stream?

Listing with an agent puts the house in front of the widest group of buyers, which suits a house in good shape and an owner who can wait through showings, inspection requests and a buyer's mortgage approval. Selling it yourself saves the agent's fee but leaves the contract, disclosures and the village stamp paperwork on your desk.

An as-is cash sale fits a house that needs work, has a tenant in it, came through an estate or faces a tight deadline. The trade-off is that a cash offer is usually below what a fully repaired house might bring on the open market. Weigh the offer against the repair bill, the carrying costs while the house sits, and the time you have.

More questions about Carol Stream, IL

Do I pay the Carol Stream transfer tax as the seller?

Usually yes. The village page says the tax generally falls on the grantor, the seller, with an exception for sheriff's sales and tax deeds, where the buyer pays. The rate shown is $3.00 per $1,000 of the price or fraction thereof.

How soon before closing should I book the water meter reading?

Book it at least two working days before closing. Call the Water Billing division at 630-871-6222. The final bill, and anything else owed to the village, must be paid before the stamp is issued.

Which school district is my Carol Stream house in?

It depends on the address. Most homes are in District 93 and Glenbard North, while parts of the village fall in U46, District 25, District 200 or District 41. Check the boundary with the district before you advertise the house.

Can I sell if a past owner skipped a permit?

Yes, you can still sell, but the issue may come up in an inspection or title review. Ask the Community Development Department at 630-871-6230 about the permit history. An as-is cash buyer may take the risk on, while a financed buyer may ask you to resolve it first.

Where is the deed recorded after the sale?

With the DuPage County Recorder, the county's land records office. The state transfer declaration and the village stamp are completed before recording. Call 630-407-5400 with questions about recording.

Quincy at a glance

Selling in Quincy?

Which way of selling fits a Quincy homeowner?

Quincy owners usually choose between a standard listing, a private sale, and a direct offer from someone paying cash for the house exactly as it stands. Age of the structure, the work it needs and your calendar decide which of those makes sense.

Quincy has several historic districts, and many of its brick homes date to the German immigrant building boom of the late 1800s. Those houses charm some buyers and put off others who dread the cost of updating them. Think through which of these describes your situation:

  • The condition is sound and months of waiting for the right buyer would not hurt, which favors a listing.
  • A roof, furnace or foundation needs money you would prefer not to spend.
  • A parent who lived there for decades has died and you are settling the estate.
  • A tenant, a code complaint or a lien is getting in the way of a conventional sale.

In the last three situations a direct sale can shorten the process, since no lender appraisal has to be passed. With any route, get the price, the closing date and the split of costs written down before you commit.

What do Census estimates reveal about Quincy housing?

Quincy prices sit low and renters make up a sizable share of households. Just 63.6 percent of occupied units are lived in by their owners in the 2020 to 2024 estimates, which gives landlords and investors a real presence among buyers.

The city has lost a little population since 2010, when the census counted 40,633 residents. The population peaked decades ago, and about one in five residents is 65 or older. Plenty of sellers are longtime owners downsizing or heirs clearing out a parent's place. Commutes average about 14 minutes, which is a point to mention to buyers.

How do the bluffs, river and neighborhoods shape a Quincy sale?

The city rises on bluffs above the Mississippi River at Quincy Bay, with a floodplain across the river in Missouri and the Quincy Hills to the east. Houses on sloping lots near the river deserve a close look at drainage, retaining walls and basement moisture before you list.

The city is compact, at about 15.8 square miles, and buyers tend to think in terms of areas. Downtown is a historic district, and the South Side German Historic District holds the brick homes built by German immigrants in the late 1800s, including the Dick Brothers Brewery buildings from 1857. North Quincy lies beyond a rail line and a large creek, and Hickory Grove sits to the east along Interstate 172.

  • Illinois Route 104 (Broadway) runs from the river bridges east to Interstate 172.
  • Illinois Route 96 doubles as the Great River Road, and Illinois Route 57 links U.S. 24 downtown to Interstate 172.
  • U.S. Route 24 crosses the river on the Quincy Memorial Bridge and the Bayview Bridge.
  • Interstate 72 passes about 12 miles south of town.

A house inside or beside a historic district should be described in terms of its architecture. Brickwork, original trim and period details are what shoppers in those areas tend to look for.

What drives Quincy's economy and demand for homes?

Quincy's largest employers anchor steady demand for housing. Blessing Hospital, Quincy Public Schools and Titan International are named as the area's top three employers. Niemann Foods, Gardner Denver, Kohl Wholesale and Knapheide Manufacturing are among the companies headquartered in town.

Higher education adds renters and buyers as well. Quincy University, John Wood Community College, Gem City College and the Blessing-Rieman College of Nursing and Health Sciences are all in or near the city, and the public school district is Quincy Public School District 172. Employers and campuses of that size keep a base of local buyers and renters in the market.

Census figures put health care and social assistance receipts in Quincy at about $1.3 billion for 2022. The Quincy and Hannibal area forms a combined statistical area of roughly 116,000 people, so some buyers come from across the river in Missouri.

What city rules should a Quincy seller check?

Quincy's Office of Inspection, on the second floor of City Hall at 730 Maine Street, handles building permits and minimum housing complaints. The city runs a complaint-driven system for rentals, where a tenant files a Minimum Housing Complaint Form and an inspector visits. If you are selling a rental, ask the Office of Inspection whether any registration or inspection requirement applies to your address.

The complaint form's checklist shows what inspectors measure against the International Property Maintenance Code. Working smoke detectors in each bedroom and hallway, carbon monoxide alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage, handrails on stairs with more than four risers, a watertight roof and a heating system that holds 68 degrees are among them. A buyer's home inspector will likely check the same points, so repair them before you list.

The city has also had a Small Rental Rehabilitation Program for owners of small rental buildings west of 18th Street, but its program page carries a note that the city is not offering it. Do not count on that money when pricing a repair-heavy house.

What local history helps explain Quincy's older housing?

Quincy was founded by John Wood and took its name in 1825, when the settlement became the seat of Adams County and honored the newly elected president. It was incorporated as a city in 1840 and grew into the second-largest city in Illinois, passing Peoria in 1870. Riverboats and rail service made it a transportation center in the 1800s.

The 2020 census counted 39,463 people, below the high of 45,288 recorded in 1970. Housing built for a larger population now serves a smaller one, with 10.4 percent of the 19,028 housing units vacant in 2020 and a rental vacancy rate of 11.6 percent. Sellers should expect buyers to compare their house with others on the market and to ask pointed questions about condition, so a clear repair history and recent utility bills help.

How does a Quincy sale get recorded in Adams County?

Adams County files deeds through its Clerk and Recorder office at 507 Vermont Street in Quincy. According to the office, a deed or trust document has to arrive with an Illinois Department of Revenue Real Estate Transfer Declaration or a Statement of Exemption.

The posted fees start at $80.00 for land records under 50 pages on standard paper, rise to $92.00 for documents that miss the 55 ILCS 5/3-5018 format standards, and add $80.00 per extra book and page reference. The table says it includes the Rental Housing Support Fee increase that began July 1, 2023. Fees move over time, so confirm the amount with the office before closing.

State law adds a duty on the seller's side: a completed residential disclosure report goes to the buyer ahead of a signed contract (765 ILCS 77/20). The following section limits that duty to material defects the seller actually knows about, with no obligation to investigate. Hold on to invoices for any work done on the house.

More questions about Quincy, IL

Does an older brick house take longer to sell in Quincy?

Often, because buyers want evidence that the wiring, plumbing and foundation are sound. A listing can reach people who prize historic detail, and a direct sale suits an owner who wants to skip the repairs.

What are the recording fees for a Quincy deed?

Adams County posts $80.00 as the minimum for land records under 50 pages that meet the paper standards, and $92.00 for those that do not. Call the office to confirm the schedule before closing.

Does Quincy require a rental registration for landlords selling a house?

The city's housing complaint process is tenant-driven, and an inspector visits after a complaint. Ask the Office of Inspection at City Hall whether any registration applies to your property before you list a rental.

Who inspects Quincy houses for code problems?

The city's Office of Inspection, at 730 Maine Street, reviews minimum housing complaints and building permits. A tenant files the complaint form and an inspector schedules a visit.

How big is Quincy?

Census Bureau estimates for 2025 give 38,918 people, down from 39,463 in the 2020 count. Quincy is the Adams County seat, on the Mississippi River.

Where is Park Ridge and how did it develop?

Park Ridge is a city in Cook County about 15 miles north of downtown Chicago, close to O'Hare International Airport. It covers roughly 7 square miles and touches three Chicago community areas on the Far Northwest Side: Edison Park, Norwood Park and O'Hare. The Des Plaines River separates it from Des Plaines to the west.

The ground itself shaped the early town. Clay deposits fed a brickworks that George Penny established in 1854, and locals called the settlement Brickton, after an earlier name of Pennyville. The city was incorporated in 1873. Population then jumped from 10,417 in 1930 to 32,659 in 1960 and peaked at 42,614 in 1970 before settling near 39,656 in the 2020 census. Much of the housing stock traces to that mid-century boom, so a buyer's inspector will look closely at the age of the wiring, plumbing, roof and foundation.

What do the Census numbers say about Park Ridge homeowners?

Park Ridge is a city of long-time owners. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates show 92.8 percent of residents living in the same house a year earlier.

With 84.8 percent of units owner-occupied, most buyers are likely to be families who plan to live in the house and who usually rely on a mortgage. A house that cannot pass a lender's appraisal or an inspection can lose that kind of buyer, which is where a cash sale enters the picture.

How do the trains and schools affect a Park Ridge sale?

Two Metra stops, Park Ridge and Dee Road, sit on the Union Pacific Northwest Line, with service southeast to Ogilvie Transportation Center and northwest to Harvard and McHenry. The CTA runs Route 68 to Chicago, and Pace operates several regional routes.

Schools are a major reason families look here:

  • Park Ridge-Niles School District 64 runs the elementary schools, including Carpenter, Field, Franklin, Roosevelt and Washington, plus Lincoln Middle School and Emerson Middle School in Niles.
  • Maine Township High School District 207 serves high school students. Maine East and Maine South are the two campuses, and students in the north part of the city can choose either.
  • St. Paul of the Cross and Mary Seat of Wisdom are the Catholic elementary schools, and St. Andrews is Lutheran.
  • The city belongs to the Oakton Community College district.

The city's 2020 financial report lists Advocate Lutheran General Hospital as its largest employer, with 3,693 employees, followed by the high school district, the Park District and District 64.

Do you need a permit for repairs on a Park Ridge house?

A permit is required for most construction. The city lists new buildings, additions, garages, driveways, HVAC, electrical and plumbing work, pools, fences, patios, decks, sheds and siding. It does not require one for window replacement unless the opening is enlarged, or for residential roof replacement, although roofing contractors must be licensed with the city. Routine maintenance that leaves existing systems and structural walls alone also needs none.

Timing matters if you plan fixes before a sale:

  • Reviews usually take up to two weeks, and the standard time is two weeks for every permit during the May to September busy season.
  • Residential permits stay valid for one year, and a renewal after expiration costs 50 percent of the original permit fee.
  • Applications go through the Civic Access online portal, and inspections are booked by morning or afternoon block with a one to two business day lead time.

Questions go to the Community Preservation and Development department at 847-318-5291. A separate tree removal permit is required for trees larger than 10 inches in diameter, so check before clearing a lot.

What does the Park Ridge transfer tax cost and who files it?

The city charges its own real estate transfer tax, and the seller pays it. The city's FAQ prints the rate as $2.00 per $1,000 of value or fraction thereof. Cook County Clerk's municipal list shows the same rate for Park Ridge, notes that it includes foreclosures, and lists the exempt-transfer fee as $25.00.

To get the transfer tax certificate, send the Finance Department:

  • The PTAX-203 or MyDec form.
  • A photo of the water meter for the final reading.
  • The closing date.
  • A contact name, phone number and email address.

Documents go to transferstamp@parkridge.us or to the Finance Department at 505 Butler Place; questions go to 847-318-5222, option 4. The certificate is issued once the tax and any other amounts owed to the city, including the final water bill, are paid, and the certificate is attached to the deed at recording. Cook County adds its own state rate of 50 cents per $500 and county rate of 25 cents per $500.

How do water bills and closing dates work in Park Ridge?

The city bills water every other month, with bills issued on the last day of the month and due by the 20th. Email the meter photo no earlier than five days before closing, with the service address and closing date. Water is not shut off during a transfer, and the account moves automatically into the buyer's name.

Final payment is accepted as cash, credit or debit card, certified check, money order or attorney's check. Homeowners are responsible for repairs to the water service pipe between the buffalo box and the house, which is worth knowing if a buyer's inspection turns up a leak. The city also says property assessment is a Cook County function, so appeals and exemptions go to the county assessor, not City Hall.

Are there landmark or preservation rules to know about?

Park Ridge has a Historic Preservation Commission. According to the city's FAQ, a house becomes a local landmark only with the owner's consent, and a designation can be rescinded, though the Commission encourages owners to look at alternatives first. If your house is already landmarked, tell buyers early.

What are your options for selling quickly in Park Ridge?

With a median owner-occupied value of $551,200 and owners who tend to stay put, a standard listing is the usual route when a house is in good shape. A cash buyer is more useful when the house needs work that would take months to finish, when a probate or move deadline is close, or when you want to avoid showings.

Before you accept any offer, line up the transfer tax certificate steps above, because closing cannot be completed without the city's certificate and the final water reading. Ask your closing attorney or title company to start those steps as soon as the contract is signed.

More questions about Park Ridge, IL

How much is the Park Ridge transfer tax?

The city's FAQ prints it as $2.00 per $1,000 of value or fraction thereof, paid by the seller. Cook County's clerk list matches that rate. The state adds 50 cents per $500 and the county adds 25 cents per $500.

Do I need to pay my final water bill before closing in Park Ridge?

Yes. The transfer tax certificate is issued after the tax and any other amounts owed to the city, including the final water bill, are paid. Email a photo of the meter to the Finance Department no earlier than five days before closing.

Can I replace my roof or windows in Park Ridge without a permit?

Usually yes. The city says residential roof replacement and window replacement do not need a permit, unless the window opening is enlarged. Roofing contractors must be licensed with the city, and other projects such as decks, fences and electrical work still require permits.

Who handles Park Ridge property tax appeals?

Cook County does. The city says assessment is a county function and refers owners to the Cook County Assessor's office, which handles appeals, exemptions and the required forms.

Does the water account transfer when a Park Ridge house sells?

Yes. The city places the account in the buyer's name automatically, does not shut off service during the transfer, and bills every other month afterward. Sellers settle the final reading through the transfer tax process.

Carpentersville at a glance

Selling in Carpentersville?

Where is Carpentersville and what is the village like?

Carpentersville is a village in northern Kane County, Illinois, on the Fox River and part of the Chicago metropolitan area. The 2020 census counted 37,983 residents in 8.09 square miles, of which 7.88 are land.

The village runs under a council-manager form of government: an elected president and six trustees appoint a professional manager who runs daily operations. For a seller, the practical point is that Carpentersville handles its own permits, water billing and rental licensing, so most of the paperwork stays at Village Hall rather than moving to a county office.

  • County: Kane, with deeds recorded by the Kane County Recorder in Geneva
  • Green space: Carpenter Park, the Carpentersville Dam area and Raceway Woods Forest Preserve
  • Housing units in 2020: 11,777, of which 2.9 percent were vacant

How did the Fox River settlement become Carpentersville?

In 1837 the Carpenter brothers were heading for the Rock River when spring floods stopped their oxcart journey on the east bank of the Fox River. They stayed and called the place Carpenters' Grove. Julius Angelo Carpenter built the first store, bridge and factory, and he later served two terms in the Illinois House.

The Illinois Iron and Bolt foundry anchored early industry, and an electric interurban line reached the foundry in 1896. For about a hundred years the town grew slowly. Until the 1950s it was a street grid along the river centered on Main Street, which was the only highway bridge across the Fox between Algonquin and Dundee.

Then the suburbs arrived. The population went from 1,523 in 1950 to 17,424 in 1960, the fastest jump in the village's history. Older homes near the river and the post-1950 subdivisions are very different housing, and a seller should know which type they own when pricing.

How has the population changed since 1950?

The census counts show one great leap in the 1950s, a flat stretch through the 1980s and steady growth into the 2000s. Growth since 2010 has been small, up 0.8 percent between 2010 and 2020.

The 2020 median age was 32.5, and 29.6 percent of residents were under 18. Of 11,439 households, 47.8 percent had children at home. That is a young, family-heavy village, so house size and layout matter to the likely buyer pool.

What do the village's housing numbers say about demand?

The 2020 census recorded a homeowner vacancy rate of 0.9 percent and a rental vacancy rate of 5.0 percent. A homeowner vacancy rate that low suggests few for-sale houses sit empty, which is generally favorable to a seller who prices the house sensibly.

The village's income section lists a median household income of $73,105 and a median family income of $79,102, with a per capita income of $26,770. Those figures help frame what a buyer who needs a mortgage can afford, and they are one reason some owners prefer a cash buyer who does not depend on lender approval.

What landmarks and shopping areas shape the village?

The Meadowdale Shopping Center opened in May 1957 and had grown to as many as 53 stores a year later. A November 1963 fire destroyed 25 stores and an ice rink, and the mall reopened in November 1964 without the rink. A competing mall opened 2.5 miles west in 1980, and Meadowdale shrank through the 1980s. Part of it was demolished in 1989, and a Walmart opened on the east end in 2016.

From 1958 to 1969 the Meadowdale International Raceway, a 3.27 mile track west of Illinois Route 31, ran here. The site is now a township park and county forest preserve. Since the 1990s, growth has moved west along Randall Road, where newer subdivisions and shopping centers sit.

The Dundee Township Historic District appears among the village's related places. If your house is in the older river-side grid, ask Village Hall whether any local review applies before you plan exterior changes.

How do people get around Carpentersville?

Illinois Route 31 runs past the older river-side grid, and Randall Road is the corridor where the newer subdivisions and shopping centers were built. Pace buses connect the village to Crystal Lake, Elgin and other destinations. A Chicago and North Western line between Elgin and Crystal Lake served Carpentersville from 1904 to 1932.

A buyer comparing Carpentersville with its neighbors will look at bus access and drive times, so mention both in a listing.

Does Carpentersville charge a transfer stamp on a sale?

No. The village's transfer stamp page says Carpentersville does not have a transfer stamp requirement for real estate transactions. This puts it among the simpler closings for a seller in the northwest suburbs.

The seller still has one task. Call the Water Billing Department at 847-551-3476 to schedule a final reading on the water meter. The new owner then opens service in person at Village Hall with a settlement statement or deed, a completed water application and picture identification.

State tax still applies. Illinois taxes the transfer of title at 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction thereof under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, based on the declaration filed for the sale.

What permits and inspections come up when selling in Carpentersville?

The Community Development Department issues permits for construction, and the village's permit page says even a new water heater or a shed needs some kind of permit or approval. It also links a list of work that does and does not need one.

  • Past work: if the previous owner added a deck, finished a basement or replaced a furnace, confirm the permit was closed
  • Open work: a buyer who takes the house as-is takes the open permit with it
  • Rental houses: the village runs a rental licensing program with an initial inspection and an annual license

The village's rental licensing checklist, last revised in 2011, describes a temporary certificate after an application, then an inspection, then a follow-up inspection if violations are found, and a Crime Free Housing seminar the owner must attend. Ask Community Development for the current version before you rely on it. If you plan to sell a tenant-occupied house, note that the owner is responsible for getting tenant consent for inspection visits.

Where is the deed recorded for a Carpentersville sale?

The Kane County Recorder in Geneva keeps the land records for the village. The recorder's website provides a records search, and the office describes services including recording, copying, scanning and a tract department.

The recorder has also announced a free Property Watch service aimed at deed fraud, which the office says targets homeowners at risk of foreclosure. An owner of a vacant or inherited house may want to look at it.

How do a regular listing and a cash sale compare in Carpentersville?

A listing makes sense when the house is move-in ready and you can wait out showings and a buyer's financing. A cash sale as-is makes sense when repairs, a tenant, an inherited estate or a deadline would make a listing slow or costly.

In either case the village side is light: no municipal stamp, a final water reading and the permit review above. That leaves the seller's time and repair costs as the real variables, so compare the net result of each route rather than the headline price.

More questions about Carpentersville, IL

Do I need a village transfer stamp to sell in Carpentersville?

No. The village states it has no transfer stamp requirement for real estate sales. You should still schedule a final water meter reading by calling Water Billing at 847-551-3476.

What does the buyer need to start water service?

The new owner brings a settlement statement or deed to Village Hall in person, fills out the water application and shows picture identification.

Is a permit needed for a water heater or shed in Carpentersville?

Yes, in general. The village's building page says work from a new water heater or shed up to a full building requires some type of permit or approval. Check the village's list of work that does and does not need a permit before you start.

Which county records the deed?

Kane County. The Kane County Recorder in Geneva records deeds and offers an online records search.

How much did Carpentersville grow in the last census decade?

Slightly. The population rose from 37,691 in 2010 to 37,983 in 2020, a gain of 0.8 percent.

Which sale method makes sense for a Rock Island owner?

Owners here can hire an agent to list the house, market it themselves, or accept an offer from a buyer paying cash who is willing to take the property as it is. Repairs, timing and whether the building is a home or a rental drive the choice.

Rock Island is one of the Quad Cities, alongside Moline and East Moline in Illinois and Davenport and Bettendorf in Iowa, so the buyer pool crosses the river. A tidy house can do well on the open market. One that needs work, carries a tenant or sits on a rental-heavy block may be better matched to a direct sale. Weigh these points:

  • Putting the house on the market reaches the most shoppers, though repairs and open-house hours usually come with it.
  • Selling privately skips the agent's commission and leaves marketing, paperwork and negotiation to you.
  • A direct purchase for cash can close without a lender's appraisal, which keeps the schedule in your hands.
  • If the property is a rental, the city's rental license and inspection rules may come into play first.

Whichever way you go, have the price, closing date and cost split in writing before you commit.

What is the Rock Island housing picture in the Census data?

Home prices in Rock Island run modest. The five-year Census survey ending in 2024 puts the middle value of a house occupied by its owner at $125,900, and roughly 35 percent of occupied units are rented.

Rock Island city, Illinois, selected figures from Census Bureau QuickFacts

The 2010 census counted 39,018 residents, and the count has slipped since. In a market like this, many sellers are landlords or heirs and many buyers are local investors. A rental should be priced with area rents in mind, because an investor works backward from what tenants pay, and the middle gross rent is $842.

How do the rivers, the Arsenal and the neighborhoods shape a Rock Island sale?

The city sits where the Rock River meets the Mississippi, and Arsenal Island, the original Rock Island, lies in the Mississippi between Rock Island and Davenport. Rock Island Arsenal is the largest government-owned weapons manufacturing arsenal in the United States and employs about 6,000 people, so the base accounts for a large part of the local job market.

The city's older pockets each have their own character:

  • Downtown and the Broadway Historic District, with well-preserved late 1800s and early 1900s buildings.
  • Watch Hill and the southern part of the city, once the separate community of Searstown and annexed in 1915.
  • The blocks around Augustana College, which was founded in 1860.
  • Streets near the Mississippi riverfront, home to Schwiebert Riverfront Park and a casino.

Rock Island is also an old rail town. The Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad was founded here in 1851. Bridges cross to Davenport, including the Government Bridge, the Centennial Bridge and the Interstate 280 bridge, and Quad Cities MetroLINK buses use District Station downtown as a hub.

Which employers and schools matter to Rock Island buyers?

In its 2017 annual financial report the city ranked Rock Island Arsenal first with 6,301 employees, ahead of Trinity Rock Island with 1,848 and Rock Island-Milan School District 41 with 1,292. County government, Jumer's Casino and Hotel, Augustana College and Modern Woodmen of America each employ several hundred more.

District 41, Rock Island-Milan, covers the bulk of the city with 13 public schools, among them Rock Island High School. Some southwest addresses belong to Rockridge. Jordan Catholic Elementary School and Alleman Catholic High School serve private-school families.

An address close to a district line deserves a call to the district before you advertise it. Plenty of shoppers narrow their search by school district before they look at streets.

What is Rock Island's history, and how does it show in older houses?

The oldest part of the city was called Farnhamsburg, after homes built in 1826 by two trading partners. A plat was filed in 1835 under the name Stephenson, and the town took the name Rock Island in March 1841. The Rock Island Arsenal has produced equipment for the U.S. Army since the 1880s and was established in 1862, and it is a National Historic Landmark.

Two hotels, the Harper House and the Rock Island House, opened during the late 1800s. Chippiannock Cemetery dates to 1854, and the public library was established in 1872. A new Rock Island County courthouse was built from 2017 to 2018 at a cost of $28 million. These details matter to a seller mostly because they show how much of the city dates from the 1800s and early 1900s. Older houses can carry original wiring, plaster and stone foundations, and a buyer will want to know what has been updated.

What does Rock Island require for rental properties before a sale?

City ordinance calls for a rental license on every residential rental, and each unit has to pass an inspection against a minimum code standard before it is offered to tenants. Landlords apply through the city's self-service portal, and the Inspection Division sends an email to schedule the inspection after the rental fee is paid.

Inspections are scheduled with the owner or a designated agent, who must be present, and a cancellation fee of $50 applies if the owner does not appear or cancel 24 hours ahead. A Notice of Violation lists items that fail life safety requirements. The first re-inspection is free, and additional compliance inspections cost $50 each. The city can fine owners and revoke the license if repairs are not made in a reasonable time.

A license does not release the owner from fixing violations. Planning to sell a rental? Clear any open violations or tell the buyer about them, and ask the Inspection Division at 1528 Third Avenue where your license stands before you list.

How is a Rock Island deed recorded and which transfers are exempt from tax?

Deeds for Rock Island parcels are recorded with the Rock Island County Recorder. The office's fee schedule, set by county ordinance effective February 1, 2025, lists $83 for a conforming document with no page count, $64 for certain exempt document types, and $104 for a non-conforming document or one with more than five references. Any document with a legal description also needs the 10-digit PIN.

The state transfer tax statute exempts a list of transfers from the tax, and some of them still require the declaration to be filed. Section 31-45 of the Property Tax Code lists these among the exempt items: deeds where the actual consideration is less than $100, tax deeds, deeds of partition, deeds that only correct or confirm an earlier deed, deeds to or from government bodies and charities, and deeds given to a mortgage holder after foreclosure or as a substitute for it. A normal sale to a buyer does not fall in these categories.

Rock Island County offers a no-cost Property Fraud Alert subscription that sends a notice whenever a filing mentions you. Someone leaving a house empty for a while may want to enroll first.

More questions about Rock Island, IL

Do I need a city rental license in order to sell a rented Rock Island house?

The license applies to renting a unit, so selling does not need one. Open inspection violations on a rented house can still slow a sale, so ask the Inspection Division where your file stands.

How much do Rock Island houses cost?

The survey figure for the middle owner-occupied home is $125,900. An individual house can land far above or below it, depending on size, condition and block.

Where is a Rock Island deed recorded?

Rock Island County. Its Recorder's Office lists conforming documents at $83 and non-conforming documents at $104 under a fee schedule effective February 1, 2025. Confirm the current figure before closing.

What school district is my Rock Island house in?

Rock Island-Milan School District 41 covers most addresses. A few in the southwest belong to Rockridge, so verify yours with the district.

How large is Rock Island?

About 36,225 people lived here in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate. Rock Island holds the county seat and counts among the Quad Cities.

Northbrook at a glance

Selling in Northbrook?
We buy Northbrook houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What should a Northbrook homeowner know before selling?

Northbrook is one of the simpler Cook County villages to sell in on paper, because it charges no municipal transfer tax and issues no transfer stamps. The one local step is closing out the water account with a final meter reading.

The village sits on the North Shore in Cook County, spreads over about 13 square miles, and borders Lake County to the north. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 34,744 residents. Housing is mostly owner-occupied and high in value, so the local process is short and most of a seller's effort goes into pricing and condition.

This page covers the Northbrook rules, the Cook County steps that apply, and how a direct sale compares with a listing.

What is Northbrook like for sellers and buyers?

Northbrook began as Shermerville, named for the man who gave land for its first railroad station, and took its present name in 1923. It was incorporated in 1901. The population climbed from 3,319 in 1950 to 30,735 by 1980, and the last working farm closed in 1987. The village was also the first community without a Lake Michigan shoreline to filter lake water for public use.

  • Several elementary districts, numbered 27, 28, 30 and 31, serve the village, and High School District 225 feeds Glenbrook North High School. A small northwest corner falls in Wheeling's District 21, and a southeast sliver is in Sunset Ridge District 29.
  • Metra's Milwaukee District North Line stops at Northbrook station on Shermer Road downtown.
  • Shopping runs along Sanders Road, Skokie Boulevard and Lake Cook Road, and Northbrook Court opened in 1976.
  • Allstate is the largest employer, and Astellas and Barilla have North American headquarters in the village.
  • The Northbrook Park District runs Techny Prairie Park and Fields, a 113-acre park along the West Fork of the North Branch of the Chicago River.

Because the school district boundaries cross house by house, a listing should name the exact elementary and junior high district for the address. The village's Know Your Neighborhood tool shows zoning and school districts by property.

What do Census numbers show for Northbrook housing?

The owner-occupied rate is 87.2% for 2020 to 2024, which makes Northbrook a house-owner village. The table below shows the figures most useful for a pricing conversation.

Northbrook housing and income, from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts table for the village.

Owner-occupied housing unit rate, 2020-202487.2%

Median gross rent, 2020-2024$2,463
Median household income, 2020-2024$157,782
Residents living in the same house a year earlier91.9%
Residents age 65 and over26.6%

A 91.9% same-house rate means few homes change hands in a given year, so comparable sales can be thin on a specific block. Ask an appraiser or agent for nearby sales, since the village median hides block-by-block differences.

Does Northbrook charge a transfer tax or require transfer stamps?

No. The village states on its real estate agent page that it does not levy a real estate transfer tax or issue transfer stamps. The Cook County Clerk's municipal transfer tax list, updated October 2025, has no entry for Northbrook either.

The state and county taxes still apply. The Clerk lists the State of Illinois rate as 50 cents per $500 and the Cook County rate as 25 cents per $500, with the seller as the liable party. The state rate comes from 35 ILCS 200/31-10. A sale also needs the PTAX-203 transfer declaration.

What does the village require for the water account?

Northbrook Municipal Code Section 27-63 requires everyone in a property transaction to confirm with the village that a final meter reading was taken and that no unpaid water balance remains. Call the water billing office at 847-664-4171 to set that up.

  • Water is billed quarterly, and sewer and stormwater charges ride on the same bill.
  • If the seller leaves a balance, the code ties it to the property, and it moves to the new owner's account after thirty days.
  • Sellers should close any utility accounts and schedule final reads as part of the sale, per the village's guidance to agents.

Settling the final bill at the closing table avoids a dispute with the buyer later. For liens and other debts, the village points to the Cook County Property Tax Portal and suggests a FOIA request for building permits and other outstanding items on a parcel.

How does Cook County assessment affect a Northbrook seller?

Most of Northbrook lies in Northfield Township, and a northwest corner lies in Wheeling Township. The Cook County Assessor lists both among the north suburb townships on a triennial cycle with reassessments in 2022 and 2025.

Look up your parcel's township and 14-digit PIN on the Assessor's site. The township assessor for Northfield can answer questions about an appeal. For tax installment dates and the balance on a parcel, ask the Cook County Treasurer, because the sale closing statement usually prorates the bill.

How do jobs and commuting shape demand in Northbrook?

The village counts more than 3,000 businesses providing over 45,000 jobs, more than its resident population, based on a 2018 Census Bureau estimate that Wikipedia cites. About 13% of working residents hold jobs inside the village, and roughly 87% commute elsewhere. The Census Bureau puts mean travel time to work at 26.8 minutes for 2020 to 2024.

Allstate, whose campus sits in an unincorporated part of Northbrook, is the largest employer, with about 8,000 workers. Health care, professional services, retail and manufacturing fill most of the rest. For a seller, the practical point is access: Milwaukee District North Line trains, Lake Cook Road, Sanders Road and Skokie Boulevard all matter to buyers who commute, so name them in a listing or offer discussion.

What happens when the deed is recorded in Cook County?

Northbrook deeds are recorded through the Cook County Clerk's recordings office at 118 N. Clark St., phone 312.603.5050, which also lists the state and county stamp amounts. The Clerk's list shows the seller as the party liable for the state and county tax, with a rubber stamp as proof of payment.

Because Northbrook has no municipal stamp, the closing package is lighter than in many neighboring suburbs. A seller still needs a signed deed, the PTAX-203 declaration, a clear title, and a final water read. If a trust or estate holds the title, the title company will tell you which exemption language applies.

How do I choose between listing and a direct sale in Northbrook?

With a median value above $650,000, most Northbrook houses sell through a standard listing, since buyers at that price usually arrive with a mortgage. A direct sale makes sense when the house needs more work than a listing can absorb or a family needs a quick, quiet close.

  • Choose a listing when the house is updated and you can wait for showings.
  • Choose a direct cash sale when the property is dated, a tenant or estate issue slows a listing, or you need a firm closing date.
  • Either way, arrange the final water read, confirm liens through the Cook County portal, and order the PTAX-203.

More questions about Northbrook, IL

Does Northbrook have a real estate transfer tax?

No. The village says it does not levy a transfer tax or issue transfer stamps. State and Cook County transfer taxes still apply on the deed.

What must I do about the water bill when I sell?

Call 847-664-4171 to schedule a final meter reading and pay the balance. Section 27-63 of the municipal code requires the final read, and any unpaid amount moves to the new owner after thirty days.

Which school districts serve Northbrook houses?

Elementary districts 27, 28, 30 and 31 serve most of the village, and District 225's Glenbrook North High School serves most of it. Small areas fall in Wheeling's District 21 or Sunset Ridge District 29, so check the exact address.

Which township assessor handles my Northbrook property?

Most of the village is in Northfield Township and a corner is in Wheeling Township. Look up your PIN on the Cook County Assessor's site to confirm the township.

How do I check for liens before listing?

Use Cook County's Property Tax Portal to search for liens or debts on the parcel. The village notes the county's records may not be complete, so it suggests a FOIA request for other debts and building permits.

Sell Your North Chicago House for Cash

North Chicago at a glance

Selling in North Chicago?

How does a house sale work in North Chicago, Illinois?

A North Chicago sale runs through two layers of paperwork: the city's own transfer stamp and sale inspection, then the Lake County Clerk's recording desk. An owner can hire an agent, go it alone, or take a direct offer from a buyer willing to accept the property in its present shape.

North Chicago is a Lake County city of about 8 square miles on the Lake Michigan shore, directly south of Waukegan. The latest Census Bureau estimate, dated July 2025, is 34,050 residents, up from 30,759 counted in 2020. The Great Lakes naval training center sits inside the city, and the Census Bureau counts 2,653 veterans among residents for 2020 to 2024.

The city's rules matter more than usual for a seller. A sale cannot close with a stamped deed until the city has checked for unpaid bills and, for any building, completed a sales inspection. Starting that process early keeps a closing date from slipping.

What shapes a sale in North Chicago?

The city grew around industry and the Navy. Land speculators moved in during the 1890s, a railroad depot opened in 1892, and the Washburn and Moen barbed wire plant became the first big employer. The settlement incorporated as a village in 1895 and as a city in 1909, and the Navy created its training area in 1911. A veterans hospital followed in 1926.

The population peaked in the 1970 census at 47,275 and fell to 30,759 by 2020. A few facts shape how a house here shows:

  • North Chicago Community Unit School District 187 runs the public schools, and North Chicago High School is the city's high school.
  • Two Metra stations, North Chicago and Great Lakes, serve the Union Pacific North Line, with trains south to Chicago and north to Kenosha. Pace buses link the city to Waukegan.
  • Main roads include Sheridan Road, Green Bay Road, Waukegan Road, Skokie Highway, Buckley Road and the Tri-State Tollway.
  • Foss Park Beach on the lakefront and the Greenbelt Cultural Center and Forest Preserve are the best-known green spaces.
  • Rosalind Franklin University of Medicine and Science, home of the Chicago Medical School, is among the city's larger institutions.

Most of the city drains toward the lake, while the western edge drains to the North Branch of the Chicago River. Ask the building department about any past drainage or basement water complaints on your street before you list.

How many North Chicago homes are owner-held, and what are they worth?

Roughly one home in three is owner-held, 32.6% across the five survey years ending 2024. The table below shows the housing and income figures a seller is most likely to be asked about.

Housing and income in North Chicago, from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts table for the city.
MeasureFigure
Residents, 2025 estimate34,050
Share of homes owner-held32.6%
Middle value of owned homes$159,600
Typical monthly rent$1,426
Number of households7,036
Typical household income$60,172
Land area7.99 square miles

These are citywide medians. Any one house may land far from these medians, so a closed sale on your own street is a better guide than the citywide number.

What steps does the city require before I can sell?

The city requires a transfer stamp on every sale inside its limits, and the stamp is released only after debts are cleared and the sale inspection is done. The Economic and Community Development page lays the order out this way:

  1. Call the Comptroller's Office at 847-596-8600 and the Department of Economic and Community Development at 847-596-8650 to request an outstanding payment and lien check.
  2. Pay anything the check turns up. The stamp is not issued until those payments are made.
  3. If the property has a building on it, schedule the sales inspection with Economic and Community Development.
  4. After the inspection, the buyers sign a Buyer's Acknowledgement form and give it to the Comptroller's office, which issues the stamp.
  5. The stamp goes on the deed, and the buyer or seller records the deed with the Lake County Recorder.

The department also recommends a Zoning Verification Letter before a sale. It states whether a use or structure is legal nonconforming, which can answer a buyer's questions about an old garage, an extra unit or a converted basement. The request form goes to the Economic and Community Development office at City Hall.

The building department phone is 847-596-8650, and permit questions go to permits@northchicago.org. Review times for permits are described as about 10 business days when volume is normal, so ask about timing if the inspection turns up work that needs a permit.

What do Illinois and Lake County charge on a deed?

Section 31-10 of 35 ILCS 200 sets the state tax at 50¢ for each $500 or fraction of $500. Lake County adds 25¢ per $500 on top, and its pamphlet notes that the county issues one stamp covering both. The Lake County Clerk collects the tax at recording, and the contract decides whether buyer or seller pays it.

North Chicago is one of the municipalities the county names as requiring its own stamp or exemption letter before the deed is submitted. You must get that from the city first.

  • A sale needs the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, form PTAX-203, completed through the Department of Revenue's MyDec site.
  • A deed with consideration of $100 or less carries a signed exemption statement instead of the declaration.
  • Only the stamped deed is recorded. The PTAX-203 goes to the county assessment office.
  • Recordings are filed at the Lake County Clerk's Recording Division, 18 N County St, 6th Floor, Waukegan. The office number is 847-377-2575.

The county's own pamphlet shows a $100,000 sale as an example of how the two rates combine, with a total tax of $150. Ask the Clerk's office for the figure that applies to your deed.

Do landlord and short-term rental rules affect a sale here?

Yes, if the house has ever been rented. Any dwelling not occupied by its owner falls under the landlord license rules in City Code Title 5, Chapter 14, whether or not rent is charged. The license runs January 1 to December 31, and inspections must be passed every two years for the certificate of compliance.

Other city rules that show up at closing time:

  • Short-term rentals need an endorsement on top of the landlord license, and only 25 endorsements are available per year, first come, first served.
  • Short-term rentals also owe the city's 9.5% hotel and motel tax, remitted monthly.
  • Rental properties with four or more units must have a Knox Box key box for Fire Department access under City Code Title 3, Chapter 2, Section 14.
  • Vacant and foreclosed properties must be registered through the HERA Property Registry, with a fee.
  • The city adopted the 2021 International Building, Residential, Mechanical, Fuel Gas, Fire, Property Maintenance and Existing Building codes on October 1, 2024, along with the 2020 National Electric Code.

An inherited house with a former tenant, or a house the owner has left empty, is the most common place these rules trip up a sale. Find out from the building department whether the address is registered, ideally before an offer arrives.

How are Lake County property taxes handled at closing?

Lake County sends one bill with two installment coupons. For the 2025 tax year, bills were mailed May 1, 2026, the first installment was due June 4 and the second September 4, with penalty interest added the day after each date. The county publishes a new calendar each year, and the Treasurer's office can tell you which installments are paid on your parcel.

At closing, the title company usually splits the year's tax between buyer and seller. Bring the latest bill to the closing table and phone the Lake County Treasurer if any installment shows as open. An unpaid installment stays attached to the parcel and becomes the next owner's problem unless it is settled in the closing statement.

Which way of selling suits a North Chicago house?

The choice depends on condition, timing and what the sales inspection might find. A public listing reaches the most buyers but adds showings, repair requests and a longer timeline. A direct cash sale moves faster and accepts the house with its flaws, and it still goes through the same stamp, inspection and recording steps.

  • Hire an agent and list publicly if the house shows well and you can wait for a financed buyer.
  • Sell as-is when repairs, a code violation, a former tenant or probate paperwork makes a normal listing hard.
  • Get the lien check and sales inspection started first in either case, because both can reveal debts or defects that change the price.

More questions about North Chicago, IL

Do I need a city transfer stamp to sell in North Chicago?

Yes. The city requires a transfer stamp on any sale inside its limits, and it will not issue one until outstanding payments and liens are cleared and, for a building, the sales inspection is done. The stamp is attached to the deed before it is recorded.

Which office handles the sales inspection?

Call the Department of Economic and Community Development at 847-596-8650 or write to permits@northchicago.org. The Comptroller's Office at 847-596-8600 handles the lien and payment check and issues the stamp after the buyers sign the Buyer's Acknowledgement.

What is the Illinois and Lake County transfer tax rate?

Illinois takes 50¢ per $500 and Lake County takes 25¢ per $500, both collected by the Lake County Clerk when the deed is filed. The city stamp is separate, so confirm its amount with the Comptroller's Office.

Can I sell a North Chicago rental house with tenants in it?

Yes, but the unit must be covered by a landlord license, since any dwelling not occupied by its owner falls under City Code 5-14. Ask the building department for the certificate of compliance status, because a buyer or lender may want to see it.

Where does the deed get filed after closing?

Filing happens at the Lake County Clerk's Recording Division, 18 N County St, 6th Floor, Waukegan, phone 847-377-2575. The stamped deed is the document filed, while the PTAX-203 declaration is forwarded to the assessment office.

Which selling routes are open to an O'Fallon, Illinois homeowner?

O'Fallon owners can go with an agent, run the sale themselves, or accept an offer from a company that buys for cash. The right pick turns on the house's condition, the lender's timeline and how much repair work the owner is willing to manage.

This O'Fallon sits in St. Clair County, east of St. Louis, and should not be mixed up with the O'Fallon in St. Charles County, Missouri. Both belong to the St. Louis metro area, which makes the pair unusual. The count in 2020 was 32,289 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 32,656.

  • An agent listing makes sense when the house is ready to occupy and similar sales nearby are easy to find.
  • A sale by owner works when you have the time to show the house and handle paperwork with a title company.
  • A cash purchase works for deferred maintenance, a leased rental, or an inherited property. Get any offer in writing and set it beside a listing price minus commission and repairs.

How old are O'Fallon's houses, and where did the growth come from?

O'Fallon began as a railroad town in 1854, and suburban growth picked up in the 1980s and again after Interstate 64 was widened in the 1990s, so much of the housing stands in subdivisions from those decades. Lots were platted around a Baltimore and Ohio depot and sold at public auction on May 18, 1854, and German settlers came for the farmland.

It was incorporated as a village on January 27, 1874, and voters changed to a city form of government on March 14, 1905. Population rose from 7,268 in 1970 to 12,173 in 1980, 21,910 in 2000 and 32,289 in 2020. Subdivision names that come up in listings include Thornbury Hill, Nolin Creek Estates, Fairwood Hills, Deer Creek, Forest Hills and Fairwood East.

The city seal carries a pick and shovel for the coal mines that mattered to the local economy for more than a century, a locomotive for the railroad, and planes for Scott Air Force Base.

Where is O'Fallon, and why does Scott Air Force Base matter to sellers?

O'Fallon is about 5 miles from Scott Air Force Base and roughly 17 miles from downtown St. Louis, which puts a major employer within a short drive. The city center is around two miles east of where Interstate 64 meets U.S. Route 50.

The city flag credits the base as a workplace for many residents, both military and civil service. Sellers who deal with a buyer moving on orders should keep repair receipts, appliance manuals and a recent utility history ready. The Census Bureau lists 4,679 veterans in O'Fallon for 2020-2024.

McKendree University is about 10 miles away. The city covers 15.56 square miles of land (2020), with a density near 2,075 people per square mile.

Which school districts cover O'Fallon homes?

Three districts overlap in O'Fallon: Community Consolidated School District 90, Central School District 104 and O'Fallon Township High School District 203. Buyers often ask for the district first, so print the correct one on your listing sheet.

District 90 runs five elementary schools named Delores Moye, Estelle Kampmeyer, J. E. Hinchcliffe Sr., Laverna Evans and Marie Schaefer, and two junior highs, Amelia V. Carriel and Edward A. Fulton. The high school is O'Fallon Township High School, whose main campus is on South Smiley Street and which has a separate freshman campus called Milburn. Private options include Discovery School, St. Clare Catholic School and First Baptist Academy.

Is an occupancy permit needed in O'Fallon when ownership changes?

Yes. The city requires an occupancy permit when the ownership or occupancy of a home changes and no current permit is on file, and a residential permit costs $75 as of May 1, 2025 and stays valid for two years.

The city treats the permit as a property maintenance inspection. After you apply, the schedule runs like this:

  • Call to book the inspection appointment within 7 days of applying.
  • Plan on the inspection taking place inside a month of the application.
  • Any violations must be fixed, and the permit follows within a second 30-day window after that first inspection.
  • Water and electricity must be on during the inspection.

The house may be occupied before the inspection as long as no life safety problems exist. Ameren Illinois and the city's utility billing office ask for the occupancy permit number before they open service. The city offers a seller's and a buyer's "as is" letter, and you should ask your lender whether the permit is a condition of closing. You can apply online, by mail, through the white drop box in the parking lot, or at Community Development inside City Hall. Paying by card adds a 2.35% convenience fee. Landlords are also pointed to the city's Crime-Free Rental Housing Program.

How do I stop or transfer water service in O'Fallon?

Fill out the city's start or stop service request form, and call Utility Billing at 618-624-4500 extension 1 if you need help. The office is at 255 S Lincoln Avenue and keeps weekday hours, 7 a.m. to 5:15 p.m.

The city bills water and sewer for most O'Fallon addresses and for most of Fairview Heights. A new account is charged a $50 non-refundable new service fee on its first bill. Sewer charges follow an averaging rule: June, July and August sewer use is billed from the average of the October through April water consumption, with 10,000 gallons assumed for a new residence that has no history. A bill that looks too high can mean a leak, and the city will re-read a meter and run a leak check on request.

When are St. Clair County property taxes due?

Property tax in St. Clair County comes due twice a year, and the bills payable in 2026 had due dates of July 1 and September 1. That year's calendar also listed bill mailing on May 26, September 18 to stay out of newspaper publication, October 30 as the final payment day, and a tax sale on November 2, 2026. All of those dates are behind us.

The Treasurer's office opens at half past eight and closes at half past four, and the posted dates carry a tentative label. Contact the Treasurer about the next bill's schedule, and have your closing agent explain how the seller's portion of this year's tax is credited at closing.

What does the Census report about housing costs in O'Fallon?

The figures describe a family-oriented, owner-heavy city, with 70.2% of homes occupied by their owners and 26.2% of residents under 18.

Do I need an occupancy permit to sell my O'Fallon house?

Usually yes, because the city requires one when ownership changes and no current permit is on file. A residential permit costs $75 and lasts two years, and your lender can tell you if closing depends on it.

How long does the O'Fallon occupancy inspection take to schedule?

Contact the city within 7 days of applying, and the inspection must occur within 30 days of the application. The permit itself follows within another 30 days after the first inspection.

Can a buyer move in before the occupancy inspection is done?

Yes, provided there are no life safety issues. The city allows occupancy ahead of the inspection, but the inspection still has to happen and any violations still have to be corrected.

St. Clair County. The Treasurer bills in two installments, and the bills payable in 2026 were due July 1 and September 1. Contact the Treasurer about the next bill.

Is O'Fallon, Illinois the same place as O'Fallon, Missouri?

No. They are separate cities in the same metro area. Illinois's O'Fallon is in St. Clair County, with 32,289 residents in the 2020 census, so make sure any records or tax searches use the Illinois city.

Where is Pekin and what is its housing like?

Pekin is the county seat of Tazewell County, on the Illinois River in central Illinois. It is the largest city in the county and the second most populous in the Peoria metropolitan area. A small part of the city lies in Peoria County, reached by a bridge over the river, which means some Pekin addresses are recorded and taxed in a different county than most of the city.

The Census Bureau counted 31,731 residents in 2020, down from 34,094 in 2010, and estimated 31,277 for July 2025. Housing here costs far less than in the Chicago suburbs: the median owner-occupied value in Palatine, for comparison, is $355,600. The table shows what the 2020 to 2024 figures look like for owners and renters.

What is Pekin's history and why does it matter to a seller?

A settler from Ohio built a log cabin on a ridge above the river in 1824, and a surveyor laid out the town site in 1827. One account says the name Pekin came from a nineteenth-century habit of naming towns after places thought to lie on the opposite side of the globe. The first post office opened in 1832.

Coal mining left a physical mark. Wikipedia lists at least four mines: the Pekin, Regal, Tazewell and Ubben mines. One of them, run by the Pekin Coal Mining Company until 1952, lay under what later became Broadmoor Junior High, Willow Elementary and Schramm School. The Regal mine crossed Broadway in the eastern part of town, below what is now Parkway Golf Course and Coal Miner's Park. Coal mining in Pekin had ended by 1951.

If a buyer asks whether your lot sits over old workings, the title company or the county recorder's records are the place to start. Do not guess at the answer in a listing.

Which employers and schools shape the Pekin market?

Pekin is home to the headquarters of Pekin Insurance and to the Federal Correctional Institution, Pekin, and it has its own hospital, Carle Health Peoria - Pekin Hospital. CityLink buses on Routes 17, 18 and 23 connect the city to downtown Peoria. The Census Bureau puts the average commute at 21.7 minutes.

Public schools depend on where the house sits:

  • Most of the city is in Pekin Public School District 108, which has six elementary schools, two intermediate schools, two junior highs and the Pekin Technical Education Center.
  • Parts of the Tazewell County side belong instead to North Pekin-Marquette Heights School District 102 or Rankin Community School District 98.
  • All of Pekin in Tazewell County feeds Pekin Community High School District 303.
  • The Peoria County portion is in Hollis Consolidated School District 328 and Limestone Community High School District 310.

Ask the district for the boundary of your address before a buyer does.

How do Pekin's weather and river location affect a house?

Pekin has a hot-summer continental climate. NOAA normals for 1991 to 2020 show about 37.4 inches of precipitation a year, spread through the seasons with late spring the wettest, January afternoons near 33 degrees and July afternoons near 86. Summers are humid, and winters can turn severely cold and snowy.

The river adds a flood question. The city takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program and says properties below the 1 percent annual chance flood level may be required by law to carry flood insurance. An owner who thinks the flood designation is wrong can ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Amendment, and lenders may still require insurance. Properties along the Illinois River are often subject to floodway rules. For a sale, find out your flood zone early, since it affects a buyer's mortgage and insurance.

What does Pekin require for permits and yard rules before a sale?

Pekin's Inspections Department says permits are required for electrical, plumbing, sewer, heating, ventilation and air conditioning work, and also for fences, sheds, new homes, additions, decks, signs and pools. A roofing permit applies to a complete tear-off or a second layer of shingles. Siding, windows, doors and interior remodeling need none unless the work changes structural walls, plumbing or electrical.

Other rules a buyer's agent may bring up:

  • A homeowner may do their own work but must still get a permit. The city defines a homeowner as the person who owns and lives at the residence.
  • Pools deeper than 24 inches need a permit and may sit only in the rear yard.
  • Chain link fences are not allowed in any front yard, and corner lots must keep sight lines clear.
  • Vehicles may not be parked in yards or the right of way, and must stand on a hard surface such as concrete or asphalt.

The Inspections Department takes questions at 309.478.5364. If you built a deck or finished a basement without a permit, ask whether it can be inspected before you list.

Which county records a Pekin deed, and who collects the taxes?

Most Pekin parcels are in Tazewell County, where the County Clerk and Recorder keeps real estate records. The office says everything in the Recorder's files is public record, that anyone may look through it free of charge, and that it supplies some forms at no cost. Ask the office for current recording fees and transfer stamp amounts before closing, since they change.

Parcels in the Peoria County portion go through Peoria County instead. That county's land records page says it participates in the state's MyDec system, which lets filers submit the PTAX-203 transfer declaration electronically before a deed is recorded. Check your tax bill or parcel number to see which county applies, and tell your closing attorney if the house straddles the line.

How do homeowners sell quickly in Pekin?

The median value of owner-occupied homes in Pekin is $120,700, so repair costs can take a large share of the price. A new roof or furnace is a bigger decision when the house is worth a fraction of what homes cost in Chicago's suburbs. For that reason many sellers weigh a cash purchase against listing and fixing the house first.

  • Pull any permits or inspection records so a buyer can see what was done.
  • Confirm your flood zone and your school district boundary.
  • Ask the title company which county records your parcel and whether any liens or unpaid taxes are on file.
  • Compare offers by what you keep after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not by headline price.

More questions about Pekin, IL

Which county is Pekin in?

Pekin is the county seat of Tazewell County. A small part of the city extends into Peoria County, so parcels there are recorded and taxed through Peoria County. Check your parcel number to see which applies.

Do I need a permit to replace a roof in Pekin?

Yes, for a complete tear-off and replacement, or for adding a second layer of shingles. The city's Inspections Department says siding, window and door replacement do not need a permit unless structural, plumbing or electrical changes are involved.

Does Pekin have flood rules that affect a sale?

Yes. The city takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program, and properties below the 1 percent annual chance flood level may be required by law to carry flood insurance. New construction in a flood hazard area must set the lowest floor two feet above base flood elevation.

Can I do my own repairs on my Pekin house?

Yes, if you own and live in it, but you still need the permit. The city defines a homeowner as the person who owns and lives at the residence, and nobody may work on someone else's property unless licensed or registered with the Inspections Department.

Where do I get recording information for a Pekin sale?

Ask the Tazewell County Clerk and Recorder, whose office keeps real estate records open to the public at no charge and supplies some forms for free. For the Peoria County portion of the city, use the Peoria County land records office, which accepts the MyDec transfer declaration.
